teaser: A baby, a clown or an old man? Klee hid the answer in a flower's name.
review_notes:
Dimensions about 40.5 x 38 cm; medium given as oil on gauze mounted on cardboard.
Alternative title “Baldgreis” (soon to be an old man) and the derivation of Senecio from Latin senex.
Klee joined the Bauhaus in 1921; about fifty hand puppets for his son Felix between 1916 and 1925, around thirty surviving.
Klee as a trained violinist who played in the Bern orchestra as a boy.
The inscription at lower left is read as “Klee 1922 181”.

lesson.text: How old is this person? Go on, guess. The head is as round and bald as a baby's. The cheeks are pink. But one eyebrow is arched like that of a skeptical old professor, and the tiny mouth is pursed. You could argue for six months or eighty years.

Paul Klee wanted you stuck right there. He painted this face in 1922 and named it Senecio. That is the Latin name of a family of common weeds, groundsel and ragwort, whose flowers turn into fluffy white seed heads. The word comes from senex, “old man”, because of that white hair.
Klee gave the picture a second, German title: “Baldgreis”, which means roughly “soon to be an old man”. A face caught on the way from one age to the other.

So the round head is also a flower on a stalk: a disc on a thin neck, turning toward you like a daisy. Klee builds it from the simplest shapes a child learns to draw. One circle. A few rectangles. Two triangles. Two dots.
Strip the face down to its geometry.

lines.label: The circle
lines.text: The head is a near-perfect disc that fills most of the picture. No ears, no hair, no chin: just the outline of a ball, or a flower seen from the front.

lines.label: The split
lines.text: A vertical seam divides the face in two, the way a mask is sometimes painted half and half. Colors change sides when they cross it.

lines.label: The eye line
lines.text: Join the two red pupils: the line slopes. The right eye sits lower than the left, which is enough to make the stare slightly crooked and alive.

lesson.text: That sloping line is where the personality comes from. A perfectly symmetrical circle with level eyes would be a diagram. Klee nudges one eye down, and at once somebody is looking at you, a little warily. He once described drawing as taking a line for a walk. Here, the line gets a sense of humor.
Klee shows that a face needs very little: break the symmetry of a few plain shapes and an expression appears.

In 1922 Klee was 42 and newly a teacher. The year before, he had joined the Bauhaus, a German school that trained artists, architects and designers side by side. He taught there about color and form, and filled thousands of pages with notes on how a square, a circle or a triangle behaves next to another.

Klee was a serious violinist. As a schoolboy he already played with the orchestra in Bern, and all his life he practiced almost daily, often before starting to paint. He compared combining colors to combining voices in music.

Senecio is one of those color lessons made into a person. The whole picture stays in one family of warm tones, with orange behind and pink, yellow and white patches inside the disc, like panes in a paper lantern. Against that warmth, a few sharp accents do the acting.

lesson.title: The features
lesson.text: Four small things give the disc its character.

spots.title: A red pupil
spots.text: The eyes are almond outlines with flat red discs for pupils. No highlight, no lashes. Red eyes should be alarming, yet in all this orange they feel soft.

spots.title: Triangle brow
spots.text: Above the left eye, the eyebrow is a solid white triangle, like a little roof or a clown's painted peak.

spots.title: Curved brow
spots.text: Above the right eye, a different solution: one curved dark green stroke, the only green in the picture. Two unlike eyebrows give two moods at once, surprised and doubtful.

spots.title: The nose
spots.text: Just a thin vertical line that bends slightly, continuing the seam between the two halves of the face.

lesson.text: A triangle on one side, an arc on the other: the face literally raises one eyebrow at you. Many viewers see a performer here, a harlequin, the masked clown of old Italian comedy who wears a costume of colored patches. The patchwork collar under the chin supports that reading.

At home Klee built hand puppets for his son Felix, around fifty of them, with heads modeled from plaster, bones, nutshells and even an electrical socket. He sewed some of the costumes himself. About thirty survive.
Something is still missing from that tour. A face has a mouth, and you may have skipped right over this one. Klee made it so small that it hides among the color patches in the lower half of the disc.
Where is the mouth? It is much smaller than you expect.

spots.title: A purple stitch
spots.text: Two tiny dark purple squares, set corner to corner under the nose line. That is the entire mouth: a tight little pucker, as if the figure were about to whistle or refusing to talk.

lesson.text: The surface matters as much as the shapes. Klee painted in oil on gauze, a loose, open-weave cloth, stuck onto cardboard. The paint is scraped and patchy, so the weave shows through everywhere. The face looks worn, like an old fresco or a much-handled toy, which quietly brings the “old man” back in.

At lower left he signed it “Klee 1922” with a number, part of the careful list he kept of all his works. The picture is small, about 40 by 38 centimeters (16 by 15 inches), close to the size of a real head. It hangs in the Kunstmuseum Basel, in the country where Klee grew up.

So, how old is this person? Klee's answer seems to be: both ages at the same time, the way a seed head is already inside the flower. Next time you catch a baby frowning like a grandfather, you will know which painting to think of.

quiz.question: What is a senecio?
options: A family of plants whose name comes from the Latin for “old man”
quiz.explanation: Senecio is the Latin name of groundsel and ragwort, from senex, old man.

quiz.question: What makes the stare slightly crooked?
options: The right eye sits lower than the left
quiz.explanation: The line joining the pupils slopes, breaking the symmetry.

quiz.question: How are the two eyebrows painted?
options: One as a white triangle, one as a curved green stroke
quiz.explanation: Klee gave each eye a different kind of brow.

quiz.question: What is the mouth made of?
quiz.explanation: Two small purple squares under the nose form the whole mouth.

quiz.question: Where was Klee teaching when he painted Senecio?
quiz.explanation: He had joined the Bauhaus school in 1921.

quiz.question: What did Klee paint this picture on?
quiz.explanation: The open weave of the gauze shows through the scraped paint.

facts.text: Klee made hand puppets for his son.
facts.explanation: He built around fifty for Felix, from plaster, bones, nutshells and other scraps.

facts.text: Senecio is a large mural, taller than a person.
facts.explanation: It is about 40 by 38 cm, close to the size of a real head.

facts.text: The face in Senecio is perfectly symmetrical.
facts.explanation: The eyes are at different heights and the eyebrows have different shapes.
